video_title: The Election Risks Markets Can’t Ignore | Protect the Pile Episode 28
gist: Hedgeye's chief political strategist JT Taylor argues the 2026 midterms parallel 2006, with a Democratic wave building on inflation, energy costs, a Warsh rate hike, Canada tariffs and collapsing independent support (independents D+24), though he is below prediction-market sweep odds and wants to see if the GOP money 'red firewall' works by mid-October. The panel also weighs Iran/energy October surprises, Senate math around Fetterman and 52 seats, and a $1.15T defense baseline plus a $50-80B munitions supplemental.

insights.claim: As of September 30 (2026 recording), the S&P 500 was around 7,708, just over 1% below its all-time high, while the Russell 2000 was down more than 8% from its high and the equal-weight S&P 500 down 6%, signaling very poor breadth.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Cap-weighted index strength masks broad weakness; small/mid caps are lagging badly.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield at 5.26% is the highest in 20 years, and the host attributes small/mid-cap and equal-weight weakness to the weight of rates.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive small and mid caps remain under pressure while yields sit at multi-decade highs.

insights.claim: High-yield spreads are above 300bp for BB/B credit and CCC is around 10%, which the host calls usually kryptonite for small and mid-cap stocks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Tightening credit conditions for lower-quality borrowers are a headwind for leveraged small caps.

insights.claim: A rising dollar has made the liquidity backdrop poor, and the latest PCE print may give the Fed cover to pause in October following a rate hike unveiled under Warsh.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Fed pause vs. further hikes is the swing factor for liquidity into the election.

insights.claim: Brooks suggested the S&P 500 could 'catch up' to higher interest rates with a 5-7% selloff before November, and JT said such a drop, combined with higher rates and gas/diesel prices, would significantly help Democrats because Trump has made the stock market his own performance gauge.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutright; JT Taylor
insights.so_what: An equity drawdown into the election becomes a political as well as market risk, reinforcing a Democratic wave.
insights.quote: Trump's gauge for performance uh is the stock market

insights.claim: JT frames 2026 as unmistakably parallel to 2006, when Republicans were routed amid war, high gas prices and inflation, rather than 2002 when the president's party gained seats.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Historical analog points to a large anti-incumbent midterm swing.
insights.quote: There are parallels of course of 2026 that you they're unmistakable here.

insights.claim: Prediction markets moved sharply toward Democrats over roughly two weeks due to a confluence of inflation data, the rate hike unveiled by Warsh, a tariff fight with Canada, and a lackluster Republican convention in Dallas featuring a $5,000 giveaway that 'fell like a lead balloon'.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Macro pain plus policy missteps are driving the political repricing, not a single event.

insights.claim: Trump's approval has sunk into the low-to-mid 30s, somewhat below where Bush's fell in 2006 (40s to high 30s), while inflation may be slightly better than then; presidential approval plus the generic ballot are JT's key gauges.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Approval at or below the 2006 analog supports expectations of heavy midterm losses for the GOP.

insights.claim: Most voters make up their minds by around Labor Day, so the late flood of Republican money may be too little, too late, with persistent gas, grocery, diesel and Northeast home-heating cost pressures still weighing on voters.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Energy and affordability costs are locked in through election day, limiting late GOP recovery.

insights.claim: Democrats are deliberately running a disciplined, quiet message centered only on affordability and accountability, a playbook JT says they have never really used before, and 'accountability' signals oversight fights if they win Congress.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A Democratic Congress would likely pursue aggressive oversight/investigations of the administration.

insights.claim: Independent support for Republicans has collapsed: independent men broke over 50% Republican in 2018-2024 but are polling at 40-41% in 2026, and independent women fell from about 42% to 30-31%.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A >10-point erosion among independents is a structural signal of a Democratic wave.

insights.claim: Per Quinnipiac, independents were D+11 at the end of the 2018 midterms and R+9 in 2022, but are currently D+24.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Independent margins far beyond the 2018 blue-wave level imply potential for an outsized result.

insights.claim: JT attributes the likely Republican underperformance mainly to GOP voter malaise and despondency, citing conservative contacts saying they will stay home or vote for a Democratic House as a check.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Depressed GOP turnout rather than Democratic enthusiasm alone could drive the outcome.

insights.claim: JT cautions that likely/registered-voter polls typically undercount Republicans by 2-3 points and that voters in redder states tend to 'come home', which may be the Democrats' underestimation.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Don't over-extrapolate polls; tight races could tighten by 2-3 points in the GOP's favor.

insights.claim: Republicans hold roughly a three-seat House majority (fluctuating due to deaths and resignations), so Democrats need to win about four seats to take the House.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: The bar for a Democratic House is very low.

insights.claim: The competitive House universe has expanded from 25-35 seats to roughly 35-50, including about 18-20 pure purple seats, and the light-red side is expanding faster than the light-blue side.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Map expansion into Republican territory raises the odds of a sizable Democratic majority.

insights.claim: The Cook Political Report, one of JT's bellwethers, just called for expanding the Democratic map by 10 more seats into redder territory.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Respected handicappers are shifting toward a larger Democratic gain.

insights.claim: Republicans hold an estimated 2-3x cash advantage, including Trump's roughly $400 million PAC plus affiliated and committee PACs, and JT says Democrats' constraint on expanding the map to 50-60 seats is money.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: The GOP money 'red firewall' is the main counterweight; its effect over the next 10 days is the key tell.

insights.claim: JT is lower than most forecasters and wants to see whether the Republican money 'red firewall' works over the next 7-10 days (by around October 10-15) before calling a blowout, saying a wave is building but not yet a tsunami.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Mid-October is the window to judge whether a wave becomes a blowout.
insights.quote: I think a wave is building. I don't think we're at the tsunami just yet

insights.claim: Pennsylvania (three light-red toss-up House seats with potential coattails from a very popular Democratic governor facing a weak Republican) and Iowa (two House seats plus tight Senate and governor races, in a state Trump won by 12-14 points) are JT's House bellwethers, and an Iowa blowout would signal a long night for Republicans.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Election-night tells: watch Pennsylvania and Iowa early results for wave size.

insights.claim: JT argues most of the 25-50 competitive House seats are held or contested by centrists, so a larger Democratic majority would make Jeffries' job easier, though a smaller far-left flank would still be irritating to him.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A bigger wave paradoxically implies a more governable Democratic House.
insights.quote: The best news for Jeff is the bigger number the Democrats get in the midterms, the easier job he's going to have.

insights.claim: Speaker Johnson currently faces a 30-35 member Freedom Caucus bloc against a three-to-four seat majority, and JT expects fireworks after the midterms over the debt, the budget and defense spending with both far-left and far-right flanks in play.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Post-election fiscal fights (budget, debt, defense) are a source of market volatility.

insights.claim: Polymarket priced Democrats at a 63% chance of winning the Senate and Kalshi had a Democratic sweep at 55% as of September 30; JT prefers the lower Kalshi sweep number and is himself lower on the sweep.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK); JT Taylor
insights.so_what: JT sees market-implied sweep odds as somewhat rich.

insights.claim: JT considers prediction markets good predictors given their accuracy last cycle but worries about outside influence now that they have become mainstream.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Treat prediction-market odds as useful but potentially manipulable signals.

insights.claim: JT's polling framework after Labor Day: only use aggregates of likely and registered voter polls, treat leads like 48-44 as toss-ups within the margin of error, and view a candidate crossing 50% as the signal a race is trending their way.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A practical rule for reading late-cycle polls.

insights.claim: Democrats must defend Michigan, New Hampshire, Minnesota and Georgia; Michigan is neck and neck, New Hampshire (with Sununu back) and Minnesota (weak progressive Democratic nominee) are GOP flip hopes, and Georgia should stay Democratic.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Democratic defensive seats are the main path for Republicans to hold the Senate.

insights.claim: Republican-held Senate seats now in play include North Carolina, Alaska, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Texas; JT calls Kansas, which has not had a Democratic senator in roughly 90 years, the biggest surprise but still gives the Republican the edge there.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: The breadth of the map into deep-red states shows the scale of the shift.

insights.claim: In Ohio, a state Trump won by 12, JT thinks former Senator Sherrod Brown has the edge over Senator Jon Husted in a rematch despite heavy crypto money against Brown.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Crypto PAC money may fail to defend its preferred outcomes, a signal on crypto's political leverage.

insights.claim: JT says Texas is the most fascinating Senate race; if Talarico does not win against Paxton, he sees no chance for Democrats to make ground in Texas over the next decade, calling it the right candidate at the right time against the worst Republican candidate.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Texas result is a long-term signal for the state's political trajectory.
insights.quote: the Republicans picked the worst candidate at the wrong time.

insights.claim: Trump and Vance's visit to North Carolina was followed by a 1-2 point rise for Democrat Roy Cooper, and Paxton's camp signaled Trump's rally did not help, so JT calls Trump's campaign appearances the 'October question mark' and says no purple-seat candidate should want him.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Presidential campaigning may now be a net negative in swing races, deepening GOP downside.
insights.quote: If I'm in a purple seat, no way, no how.

insights.claim: JT says Democrats need 52 Senate seats to be comfortable because Fetterman is a wild card who votes with Republicans on Israel and some foreign policy, and a 50-50 outcome with a Democratic House and Republican Senate is his nightmare, worse than a sweep.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Split Congress (D House, R Senate) is JT's worst-case gridlock scenario, contrary to the consensus that a sweep is worst.
insights.quote: I think a worst scenario is uh a Democratic House in the Republican Senate.

insights.claim: Contrary to fears of a Democratic sweep, JT argues it would at least force budgets to get done and Trump has negotiated with Pelosi and Schumer before, so it is 'not the end of the world'.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A sweep may produce more fiscal functionality than markets assume.

insights.claim: JT does not see Fetterman as a Manchin-like dealmaker, but thinks he could amass more power by staying a Democrat while making demands in a 51-49 Senate.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A single swing senator could shape legislation in a narrow Democratic Senate.

insights.claim: JT notes Schumer is not guaranteed to remain majority leader, with Maryland Senator Van Hollen rising as a fresher face, though he bets Schumer stays.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Leadership turnover could shift Senate Democratic priorities.

themes.theme: October surprises: Iran, Hormuz and energy

insights.claim: JT's main potential October surprises are geopolitical: escalation with Iran by either side affecting the Strait or Red Sea (including the Houthis), developments in Ukraine-Russia, or another big equity index dip.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Geopolitical energy shocks are the key event risk into the election.

insights.claim: Any Iran deal would need to happen within about two weeks to help Republicans, and even then diesel and energy prices will not come down before election day due to latency in the system.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor; Brooks Cutright
insights.so_what: Energy prices are effectively locked in for voters; a deal would be optics, not relief.
insights.quote: there's just too much latency in the system for that to actually be possible.

insights.claim: JT believes Iran's leadership has Trump's number and will likely take the conservative route of waiting out the midterms to deal with a weaker Trump afterward.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Expect prolonged Gulf uncertainty rather than a pre-election resolution.

insights.claim: Sam argues Iran may get its best deal before the midterms because it is financially very tight and a post-midterm Trump with nothing to lose would negotiate harder, while sanctions relief could extend the regime's survival.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Iran's financial strain is an underweighted variable that could produce a surprise deal.

insights.claim: RPK thinks the more likely Iranian escalation is not attacking a US ship, which could rally support for action, but hitting energy infrastructure such as the East-West pipeline after flows recovered to roughly 80% of pre-war levels, sending energy markets haywire.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Energy infrastructure attacks are the asymmetric tail risk for oil and markets that think the worst is over.

insights.claim: JT expects any limited ceasefire or deal could be undermined by proxy stunts from the Houthis or Iraqi Shiite militias.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Proxy disruption makes any de-escalation fragile for energy markets.

insights.claim: Sam notes that if diesel stays elevated or rises 20-30% and Congress is gridlocked, opposition lawmakers have an incentive to keep conditions painful heading into the 2028 presidential race.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Political incentives may prolong energy/affordability pain rather than resolve it.

insights.claim: JT says Iranian inflation is the highest he has seen and the population is suffering, raising the question of whether internal pressure bursts before or after the midterms, while Trump's threats to annihilate a civilization have rallied Iranians.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Regime stability is uncertain, adding to geopolitical tail risk.

insights.claim: The tariff fight with Canada, including on Bombardier, plus diesel and fertilizer costs is creating a 'perfect storm' for farmers and border states like Iowa, making Republican candidates there wary of Trump visits.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Ag-input inflation and trade disputes are politically and economically damaging in farm states.

insights.claim: RPK notes defense stocks basically peaked when the war started and have been a disaster since, despite the consensus that depleted stockpiles must be rebuilt.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: The obvious replenishment trade has not worked; the budget path matters more than the narrative.

insights.claim: JT calls Trump's $1.5 trillion defense request untenable and expects the $1.15 trillion baseline, already through the House and a 15-20% increase over FY26, to pass with Democrats coming home in the lame duck.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A large defense budget increase is still likely, just not the full request.
insights.quote: Trump's rec request of 1.5 trillion is untenable

insights.claim: JT doubts Republicans can push the ~$350 billion gap to Trump's request through reconciliation in the lame duck, but expects a bipartisan defense supplemental of $50-80 billion to replenish munitions and cover costs of the Iran war and Ukraine.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: A $50-80B supplemental is the concrete catalyst for munitions makers.

insights.claim: Democrats traditionally demand matching domestic spending increases for any defense increase, which they won't get from a Republican Senate, setting up post-midterm budget fights.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Parity demands are the main obstacle to defense appropriations timing.

insights.claim: With defense priorities shifting toward unmanned vehicles and drones, JT expects competition among states and districts for production dollars, alongside existing shipbuilding interests in Virginia and Mississippi.
insights.speaker: JT Taylor
insights.so_what: Defense dollars are rotating toward drones; geographic politics will shape who wins contracts.
